newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's ex-premier wins presidential nomination.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's ex-premier wins presidential nomination.

text.p: Former South Korean prime minister Kim Jong-pil on Tuesday won his opposition party's nomination to run for president, vowing to eliminate corruption by introducing parliamentary democracy.
Kim, 71, head of the conservative United Liberal Democrats, joins Kim Dae-jung, leader of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics in the presidential race.
The ruling New Korea Party, battered by a recent sleaze scandal, has yet to select its nominee for the December vote.

"Only a parliamentary government system can free us from dictatorship, corruption, chaos, regional factionalism, which all stem from the presidential system," said Kim Jong-pil, a former army lieutenant-colonel who choreographed a 1961 coup which thrust the late president Park Chung-hee to power.

Despite the ruling camp's woes, political analysts say the opposition has only a slim chance of taking office as the two Kims represent to many voters an old generation of politicians stained equally by corruption.
"People see the two Kims as part of the corrupt establishment and they want something new," said Kim Byung-kook, a political science professor at Korea University.
Young voters, in particular, wanted to change a political landscape dominated for years by the two Kims and their long-time rival Kim Young-sam, the current president, he said.

In a convention of Liberal Democrats, thousands of party members filled a sports arena to give a ringing endorsement to Kim Jong-pil, a prime minister under Park who ruled the nation with an iron hand for 18 years until his assassination in 1979.
He won 2,575 votes against 554 for the one candidate opposing him, Han Young-soo.
He said the current presidential system required heavy campaign spending and provided "the source of corruption".
"I will revise the constitution to introduce a parliamentary government system...after winning the presidency," he said.
The opposition has accused President Kim of allowing favours to failed Hanbo Steel Co after accepting a huge political donations to finance his 1992 election campaign.
Hanbo Steel collapsed in January under billions of dollars of loans, revealing a web of high-profile corruption.
Kim Jong-pil ran for the presidency in 1987 when he came in fourth after former general Roh Tae-woo, Kim Young-sam and Kim Dae-jung.
Political science professor Oh Suk-hong at Seoul National University said the opposition would have to field a single candidate to improve its chances.
"That is their only chance. Without a single candidate, the opposition cannot win," said Oh.
The presidential election is set for December 18. President Kim is constitutionally barred from running for a second term.
